source.title: To model human linguistic prediction, make LLMs less superhuman

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own analysis relating next-word prediction accuracy to fit on human reading-time data, testing a downstream-predictability version of the claim with a different measure from held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: Figure 1 reports the paper's own analysis for two reading-time corpora. Other results about memory, training data, and scaling are discussion or citations to prior work, not new results in this paper.
record.test_reason: This is a perspective piece. Its only own result is Figure 1, which reproduces Oh & Schuler (2023b) on Pythia models. Figure 1 relates next-word log probability to fit with human reading times. Reading-time fit measures cognitive-model alignment, not downstream task performance. So it measures a different construct from V6, and nothing in the paper measures loss scaling (V1–V5, V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors argue that mainstream LLMs' next-word predictions are superhuman, so their fit to reading times declines as accuracy improves. They attribute this to superior long-term memory (training data, memorization) and short-term memory (decay-free context). They advocate LLMs with human-like memory and new targeted human experiments.
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes the relation between next-word accuracy and reading-time fit, rather than measuring held-out cross-entropy scaling laws or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported pattern is examined on two reading-time corpora: Natural Stories and Dundee.

fits_no_version.finding: Across Pythia models of varying size and training data, better next-word prediction first improves fit to human reading times, then worsens it. This holds on Natural Stories and Dundee (Figure 1, reproducing [26]).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM surprisal's fit to human reading times is non-monotonic in model quality. It peaks at intermediate prediction accuracy and training data, then declines as models become superhuman predictors.

record.problems: Figure 1 provides the model-level results graphically without individual numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the text. The reported relationship concerns reading-time fit and next-word accuracy, not direct scaling-law tests.
record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 labels are removed: reading-time alignment is not downstream task performance. Figure 1 is a reproduction of the authors' earlier work [26], not a new experiment. Other claims (larger models fit worse, less data aligns better) are cited from prior studies.

versions.untested_parts: The analysis concerns reading-time prediction, not other downstream tasks; it relates next-word accuracy to reading-time fit, rather than directly testing whether scale or pretraining loss predicts downstream performance.
